title: Google Details Who Can License Its Search Data In Europe via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
content:
Google has revised its documentation for the European Search Dataset Licensing Program, offering detailed information on how eligible competitors can access and license search ranking, query, click, and view data from Search in the European Economic Area.
The page, last updated on August 31, covers eligibility requirements, sample datasets, audit procedures, and important deadlines. This initiative implements the European Commission’s binding decision adopted in July under the Digital Markets Act, which mandates Google to share anonymized search data with competitors, including AI chatbots that qualify as online search engines under the law.
Licensing agreements will begin dispatching from September 17, with data samples available starting November 16.
Applicants must meet the criteria of an online search engine under the DMA and target users within the EEA. They must not be controlled by non-EEA state actors or be subject to EU sanctions.
All applicants must have an average of at least 50,000 monthly users of their search service in the EU over the past year. Additionally, they must have been providing search services in the EU for the past two consecutive years or, if they are recent entrants, have received over 50 million euros in capital investment.
Google may request supporting documents and says it will respond to expressions of interest within seven calendar days.
Eligible applicants may request samples before purchasing full dataset access.
A free sample includes 1,000 rows. A synthetic dataset with up to 10 million queries and a 5% sample of the full dataset are available for a fee.
All three samples will be accessible starting November 16.
The fees for the dataset are set on fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory terms. According to the Commission’s measures, these fees are limited to the incremental costs of data provision plus a specified rate of return.
Gaining access to the 5% sample and the full dataset starts with an independent assessment. While the smaller samples don’t require an audit, Google still carefully checks each applicant’s eligibility in advance to make sure everything is in place.
An independent auditor carefully examines the applicant’s technical setup, data storage, and workflows. The Level 1 report provides assurance that the applicant has credible plans to use the data for its own search product, and that its data protection controls are suitably designed.
To keep access open, recipients agree to ongoing monitoring by an independent assurance practitioner and need to submit regular Level 2 reports. These reports test whether the controls are working in practice. The first report is due within six months of access being granted, with future reports due annually.
These audits are important because recipients handle personal data. The Commission believes that keeping the data walled off inside the recipient’s own systems can meet the DMA’s anonymization standard, but it’s up to each applicant to demonstrate that this is done properly.
In July, I discussed the binding decision when the eligibility thresholds and overall timeline were already public.
The updated page turns the July decision into dates and process. The Level 1 audit gates the 5% sample and the full dataset, not the two smaller samples. This approach allows eligible companies to examine the free rows and the synthetic dataset before they choose to incur any audit costs.
Licensing agreements come first, with technical details on the dataset to follow.
The Commission plans to review these measures every two years. Plus, Google will need to maintain a public webpage listing all third-party search engines that access the dataset.
This transparent list is an important way to see if the data extends beyond the big-name engines to include the qualifying chatbots the decision covers.

title: How to cross-post on social media (the right way)
content:
As social media users spread their attention across multiple platforms, more brands are expanding their presence to meet them there. According to our 2026 Social Media Content Strategy report , 87% of marketers plan to show up on more networks this year.
Cross-posting on social media is an excellent strategy for reaching new audiences, but it can also multiply your team’s workload, especially if you’re tailoring content to each platform.
This guide explains what cross-posting is, when it works (or backfires) and what each platform’s native rules allow. You’ll also learn how to cross-post easily with the Sprout Social Essentials plan.
Cross-posting means publishing the same content to two or more social media networks, either simultaneously or on a network-specific schedule.
But your posts shouldn’t be identical across platforms. A good cross-posting strategy preserves the core message or creative concept while optimizing the size, caption, format, tags, media and timing for each channel.
When you cross-post on social media effectively, you get content on your brand accounts quickly, freeing up your team for more strategic tasks like planning and engaging.
The right tools simplify the process. Sprout Social Essentials lets you cross-post to up to five social profiles at once. Use the unified Compose window to customize your post’s text, media and timing for each platform—no switching tabs.
Cross-posting, reposting, repurposing and sharing all extend the reach of your social content, but they describe different actions.
Only cross-post content to networks where the topic is relevant and the format makes sense. Even then, “same content” should mean the same idea, not an untouched copy of the same post.
Exact duplication works for simple, time-sensitive updates. But for most campaigns, small changes to the hook, caption, tags, call-to-action, media and publish time give the post a better chance of meeting each audience’s expectations.
Cross-posting works well when speed and consistency matter, or when audiences have similar needs across channels. Examples of content to cross-post include:
As for cadence, cross-post as often as the content fits each network, but balance it with platform-specific posts so every feed still feels original and worth following.
Create a separate post or stick to one network only when the content relies heavily on platform-specific behavior. Skip cross-posting in the following situations:
In these scenarios, the cons of cross-posting outweigh the pros. But that doesn’t mean cross-posting is bad for performance. Just avoid sharing identical or poorly adapted posts all the time as it makes your brand look repetitive and boring.
Cross-posting makes executing and scaling a multi-channel marketing strategy effortless. These five benefits show where cross-posting has the greatest impact.
Cross-posting helps your brand reach different customer groups without recreating content from scratch every single time.
Every network has its own mix of age groups, interests, professions and behaviors. For example, the latest social media demographics show that Facebook reaches 88% of Baby Boomers, compared with 39% for Instagram and 20% for TikTok.
If you’re a sports brand targeting both older and younger customers, you can cross-post a vertical video to all three platforms, tweaking the caption to resonate more with each audience.
Publishing across multiple profiles keeps your social channels active and lets you manage engagement across these touchpoints, which consumers expect and appreciate.
In fact, the 2025 Sprout Social Index™ found that 73% of social users would buy from a competitor if they didn’t receive a response on social. While cross-posting doesn’t replace community management—you still need to monitor and reply to comments and DMs—it gives your team more time to focus on these conversations.
Plus, every channel you’re active on is an opportunity to grow your business. By cross-posting, you give customers more places to discover your products, ask questions and leave feedback.
New social media networks pop up regularly (e.g., Bluesky , Threads, Lemon8), but lean teams rarely have the resources to build a separate content strategy for each. Cross-posting makes it easier to test emerging networks by using the content you already have.
Even better: use industry research to guide your experiments. For example, Sprout’s report shows 65% of Bluesky users interact with brand content at least once a week, and text posts are their preferred brand format. Brands that want to test if Bluesky makes sense for them should cross-post an X update to the platform, with a small tweak to either the tone or the CTA.
Cross-posting keeps your accounts active and puts your content in front of more people. The more channels you use, the wider your potential pool of engaged users becomes.
Build your reach across demographics, but also across regions. For example, a global brand could cross-post the same campaign to its regional accounts, then adjust the caption and examples for each market. Doing so supports an international marketing strategy without requiring a separate campaign for every location.
The best times to post on social media vary by network. But if you cross-post using a tool that supports network-specific scheduling (e.g., Sprout Essentials), you can publish each version when its audience is most likely to see it.
For example, prepare a campaign in Compose, then schedule its LinkedIn version for 11 a.m. on Tuesday, when professional engagement peaks, and its Instagram version for 2 p.m. on the same day, when the afternoon scrollers are most active. That way, your posts stay coordinated while each one reaches its target audience at the most relevant time.
Cross-posting gets more complicated as you add more networks. A post that works on one platform is often cut off or poorly formatted on another.
Knowing the formats, native cross-posting rules and character limits by platform helps you plan a post that works across all channels. The table below offers a quick comparison.
Note: Limits may change, and third-party tools might be more restrictive than native apps. If you use Sprout, check the latest media upload limits before publishing.
Instagram and Facebook have the most direct native cross-posting relationship. Once you connect your eligible accounts in Meta, turn on automatic sharing across profiles for Stories, posts and Reels .
If you only have these two accounts, native cross-posting works well. But if you also need to coordinate your Facebook and Instagram profiles with other networks, such as LinkedIn, X, TikTok or YouTube, a social media management tool like Sprout is more convenient.
X’s 280-character standard limit often becomes the constraint when one caption is sent to several networks. Keep the main point, CTA and mentions but remember to tweak the caption if X is in the mix.
X also supports up to four images in a standard post, so a larger carousel prepared for Instagram or LinkedIn will need to be reduced or redesigned.
LinkedIn gives you more room for context, but more copy isn’t automatically better. We recommend framing your post around a business insight, lesson or outcome to resonate better with LinkedIn’s professional audience.
Also, hooks are very important on LinkedIn. Make sure your content has a strong opening if you cross-post here, and avoid copying a large block of Instagram hashtags as they look spammy.
LinkedIn also supports document posts, a native format that won’t transfer directly to most other networks. Keep those specific to your LinkedIn marketing strategy .
TikTok is one of the best platforms for cross-posting short-form vertical video alongside Shorts and Reels. But the platform is known for its unique culture and trends, so customize your captions and media for TikTok’s specific audience for maximum engagement.
Some TikTok features, such as library audio, native filters and shopping elements, must be added in the app or completed through Sprout’s mobile publishing workflow .
YouTube requires packaging as well as video. A long-form upload needs a distinct title, description and thumbnail. Shorts can be square or vertical, and can last up to three minutes, but links in Shorts descriptions and comments aren’t clickable.
Keeping these details in mind helps you cross-post your content without ending up with missing or broken elements.
Note: Sharing a YouTube link to another network promotes the original upload; uploading the video itself to another network creates a true cross-post.
Cross-posting makes your multi-channel publishing workflow more efficient, but it still requires careful planning. You need to know which parts of a post stays the same, which should change and how you’ll measure each version’s performance.
The best practices below will show you how to cross-post effectively:
The best cross-posting strategy carries the same message across networks while giving each version the right framing. Keep your main idea and asset, but adjust the hook, caption, media, hashtags, CTA and formatting to match each platform.
Why? Because people use each network differently. If you copy an Instagram caption directly to LinkedIn, you might end up with too many hashtags and not enough professional context.
Here’s how you could cross-share a report on social while tailoring some elements:
Small edits often make the biggest difference. Even if it’s just a crop, a shorter caption or the right account mention, it makes your post feel like it belongs in the feed.
Pro tip: Use Sprout’s built-in photo editor to make minor edits quickly to images before they go live on each network — no need to leave the platform.
Instead of publishing everything at once, give each version its own send time to maximize the engagement potential across all channels.
For example, your audience might use LinkedIn during morning work hours but scroll Instagram or Facebook in the afternoon. If you have insight into your audiences’ peak times, use that to guide your scheduling workflow.
Pro tip: Use Sprout Social’s AI-powered optimal send times (ViralPost ® ) to schedule each version to automatically publish at the perfect time. ViralPost ® analyzes your audiences’ historical engagement patterns and suggests active windows for different platforms.
Instead of cross-posting and calling it a day, analyze how your idea worked across channels. Comparing versions tells you which platforms deserve original content and which perform well on adapted copy. This is useful when planning future content.
Remember to measure each version against its objective and platform norms. The best metrics would vary for each network, but commonly include reach or impressions, video views and watch time, engagement rate, link clicks, conversions and audience growth.
Pro tip: Use Sprout Essentials to consolidate metrics and get a “big picture” view. Generate cross-network reports for comparing profile and post level performance side by side.
Rewriting captions for every network when cross-posting takes time and creative energy, which most small teams are already short on. Instead of resorting to copy-paste captions, use AI to quickly tweak your first drafts and tailor them for each channel.
Pro tip: This is where Sprout’s Suggestions by AI Assist come in handy. If you ever get stuck, write out a rough caption idea, then generate three alternatives or try a different tone.
The Sprout Social Essentials plan centralizes your entire cross-posting workflow. You can connect up to five social profiles, customize posts for each network, schedule them to go live automatically at different times and compare their performance afterward.
Managing multiple social media accounts is time-consuming, but cross-posting is a reliable way to streamline and scale the process. When you post to all social media at once, compare performance side by side, which is useful for further optimizing your strategy.
The Sprout Social Essentials plan brings your entire cross-posting workflow into one platform. Create posts, customize per network, publish automatically with AI, measure success and more

Cross-posting means publishing the same content on two or more social media networks. Post each version simultaneously or follow a network-specific schedule.
What’s the difference between cross-posting and sharing?
Cross-posting publishes your own content across multiple profiles you control. Sharing distributes an existing post (someone else’s) through a network’s native share feature.
No, cross-posting isn’t inherently bad for performance. Engagement drops when you publish identical content too often without adapting it to each platform’s audience or features.
Cross-post when the topic and format suit several networks. Create separate posts when the content depends on a native feature, platform-specific trend or audience expectation that won’t translate well elsewhere.
Yes, cross-posting is allowed as long as you own the content or have permission to use it and follow each platform’s rules. Avoid reusing copyrighted media or watermarked videos without the necessary rights.
What type of content should you cross-post, and how often?
Announcements, evergreen tips, research findings and short-form videos are strong candidates for cross-posting. Cross-post whenever the content fits each network, but mix in platform-specific posts to keep your feeds distinct.
How should you edit a post when cross-posting across platforms?
Adjust the hook, caption length, hashtags, mentions, CTA, media dimensions and publish time for each platform. Use a tool like Sprout Social Essentials to customize posts per network when cross-posting or scheduling content.
